title: Why your stored food failed.
description: Handling history decides first, then the batch, container, absorber and closure. What the published sources document about each — and what they do not.

faq.question: The bag never sucked down. Did the oxygen absorber fail?
faq.answer: Not on that evidence. An absorber removes oxygen, which is about 21 percent of air — “1/5 of the air volume will be gone but 4/5 of the air will always remain” [39]. Wallaby Goods states that “It’s a misconception that a ‘vacuum-packed’ look confirms the oxygen has been removed” [48], and Discount Mylar Bags notes that powders and some freeze-dried items will not shrink at all [42]. No source in this set offers suck-down as a verification method; the published checks are mechanical — pull the cooled mouth open [36] or bend the cooled seal and watch for separation [54].

faq.question: The food looks and smells fine. Can I eat it?
faq.answer: Appearance does not answer that question. Penn State Extension states that “We cannot see, smell, or taste pathogenic microorganisms but we can see or smell some signs of food spoilage” [8]. FoodSafety.gov instructs, plainly, “Never taste food to determine its safety” [6], and Virginia Cooperative Extension publishes the same rule [7]. Utah State adds the mechanism for freeze-dried food specifically: freeze-drying does not kill bacteria, it preserves them dormant, and moisture can reactivate them [1][2]. Decide from handling history, and discard when history is unknown [6][16].

faq.question: Can I re-dry a batch that took on moisture and repack it?
faq.answer: Six extension services publish that permission — NCHFP, Clemson, Colorado State, Iowa State, PNW and Virginia Tech [10][11][12][13][14][15] — with NCHFP’s wording the clearest: “Foods affected by moisture, but not spoiled, should be used immediately or redried and repackaged” [10]. Every one of them gates it on the absence of mold [10][11][13][14]. Two limits: all six were written about condensation in dehydrated food, not about a failed absorber or a lost seal, and none of them covers food that was packed above 10 percent moisture under reduced oxygen — that case carries a botulism warning and a discard [46][68].

faq.question: My bag has a clear window. Is that the problem?
faq.answer: Possibly, and the reason is the foil rather than the light. PackFreshUSA states that “It is only the aluminum on the surface that keeps the oxygen out” [35], and Discount Mylar Bags says the foil layer “provides the bulk of protection in a Mylar bag” [34]. Window pouches do not have foil across the window: IMPAK flags one of its own kraft window pouches with “This product does not have foil lining” [31], and ULINE’s kraft window barrier pouch is Paper/PET/NY/LLDPE [32]. Utah State’s specification for freeze-dried storage is 5 to 7 mil mylar with no clear plastic window, plus an absorber [1].

faq.question: How much does storage temperature actually matter?
faq.answer: Utah State publishes the only rate rule found: “For every 10.8 degrees in temperature rise you decrease the shelf life of stored food by half,” with a 40 to 60 °F storage range [64]. Clemson states storage time decreases significantly above 75 °F [16]. The measured case is dried milk: unacceptable to a sensory panel at 24 months at 90 °F, at 4 years at 70 °F, with minimal flavor change at 52 months at 50 °F [66] — against chart figures of 15 to 20 years for the same product [68][69]. The rule is published as a bare assertion, with no stated valid range and no underlying data [64][65].

howTo.name: Answer the history questions before opening anything
howTo.text: How long was it out and at what temperature [4][5]; did anything raw go in [3]; was the food below 10 percent moisture when it was packed [46]. If any answer is unknown, the published guidance is to discard [6][16].

howTo.name: Look for mold and off odor, and stop there if you find either
howTo.text: “Moldy foods should be discarded” [10]; “If there is any sign of mold, discard the product” [13]; PNW adds that some toxic molds grow at room temperature [14]. Colorado State treats an off odor the same way [12].

howTo.name: Identify what the container actually is
howTo.text: Check whether there is foil across the whole bag. A clear window means no foil there [31][32], and a vacuum-sealer film publishes an oxygen transmission rate orders of magnitude above a foil laminate once the units are converted [28][27].

howTo.name: Open one absorber and feel it
howTo.text: A spent absorber is “brown and clumped together compared to a fresh pink or gray powder” [46]; PackFreshUSA’s check is that a viable one feels soft and powdery rather than hard and crunchy [41]. Do not treat bag shrinkage as evidence either way [48][56].

howTo.name: Inspect the seal by hand as well as by eye
howTo.text: FDA’s method is to rub thumb and forefinger around the seal area feeling for folds and ridges, under proper illumination [59]. Then pull the cooled mouth open [36] and bend the cooled top to see whether it separates [54]. Visual inspection alone is operator-dependent [61].

bodyHtml:
The short version: settle how the food was handled before you inspect it, because the symptoms you can see do not report on the ones you cannot. Utah State Extension states that “Freeze-drying does not kill bacteria…they can survive the freeze-drying process” [1], and that dormant organisms can reactivate when moisture is reintroduced, “such as during rehydration or improper storage” [2]. Once history is settled, work through four things in order: the batch, the container, the absorber, and the closure.

This page describes what published sources say and what they decline to say. It is not a safety clearance for any specific bag, and no test on it establishes that a food is safe to eat.

Decide before recovery — handling history

Federal guidance puts disposition on elapsed time rather than condition. USDA FSIS defines the danger zone as 40 °F to 140 °F, states that bacteria can double in as little as 20 minutes in that range, and instructs that food is never left out of refrigeration over 2 hours [5]. For perishable food left at room temperature the rule is the same: throw it away after 2 hours, or 1 hour when the ambient temperature is above 90 °F [4]. The FDA Food Code sets a parallel limit for food held under time rather than temperature control — four hours from removal, then disposal [23].

Those rules are written for refrigerated and frozen food, not for a mylar bag on a shelf. What carries across is the logic: history decides, and an inspection cannot overturn it. FoodSafety.gov states it in five words — “Never taste food to determine its safety.” [6] Virginia Cooperative Extension publishes the same instruction and adds not to consume food that develops an off odor, visible mold, or unusual appearance [7]. Penn State Extension explains why the absence of those signs proves nothing: “We cannot see, smell, or taste pathogenic microorganisms but we can see or smell some signs of food spoilage” [8]. USDA FSIS adds a second-order problem for dried product specifically — “After drying, bacteria become much more heat resistant” [9] — so a survivor in a dried food is harder to kill than the same organism was going in.

Question about the food’s historyWhat the published rule saysWhere it leaves youSource
Was it out of refrigeration, and for how long?2 hours, or 1 hour above 90 °F, then discard — for perishable foodTime governs, not appearance[4][5]
Did anything raw go into the bag?Food traditionally cooked before eating must still be cooked as a freeze-dried food — raw meats, seafood, eggs, and foods containing themThe cook step moves to consumption; it did not happen in the dryer[3]
Was the food above 10 percent moisture when it was packed under reduced oxygen?Foods should be below 10 percent moisture for storing with absorbers; high-moisture food in reduced-oxygen packaging carries botulism riskDiscard — this is a history question, not an inspection one[46][42][68]
Is there visible mold?“Moldy foods should be discarded”; “If there is any sign of mold, discard the product”; some toxic molds grow at room temperatureDiscard — no source permits salvage[10][11][13][14]
Is there an off odor?“Discard all foods that develop off smells or flavors or show signs of mold”Discard — Colorado State promotes odor to a disposition trigger[12][7]
Moisture present, no mold, no off odor?“Foods affected by moisture, but not spoiled, should be used immediately or redried and repackaged”Recovery is permitted, conditionally — see the limits below[10][11][12][13][14][15]
Any uncertainty at all?“When in Doubt, Throw it Out!”Discard[6][8][16]

Six independent extension services publish the re-drying permission — NCHFP [10], Clemson [11], Colorado State [12], Iowa State [13], PNW [14] and Virginia Tech [15] — and every one of them gates it on the absence of mold. Two limits belong here rather than in a footnote. First, all six were written about condensation and moisture pickup in dehydrated food, not about a failed oxygen absorber, a container that lost its seal, or food held above a stated temperature. Extending them to those events would be inventing a position none of the six takes. Second, none of them addresses a food that was packed wet in the first place; that case is answered by the reduced-oxygen botulism rule above [46][68], and it is answered with a discard.

Review the batch

Water activity is where the published numbers are. Clemson HGIC gives the growth minima: spoilage bacteria above 0.95; Salmonella, Vibrios and Clostridium botulinum at 0.91 or above; Staphylococcus aureus above 0.85; most molds and bread yeasts at 0.80; dry-tolerant molds at 0.70 [22]. The FDA Food Code excludes a food from time/temperature control for safety when its water activity is 0.85 or less [23], and USDA ARS publishes 12-plus months of shelf life as requiring aw below 0.6 [70]. Correctly freeze-dried product sits well below all of that — Penn State gives a range of 0.08 to 0.330 [24] and Utah State says approximately 0.3 or below [1] — which is exactly why a batch that never reached that range is the first thing to rule out.

Texture is not the test people take it for. In every jerky document checked, the bend test describes doneness and the safety determination is routed to internal temperature instead [20][21]. Utah State does use a crisp or breakable texture as a dryness criterion in safety terms for freeze-dried food, noting that correctly dried fruit “may be flexible, but not sticky” [3] — a framing difference the sources do not reconcile.

Fat is the other batch-level variable, and it runs the opposite way from intuition. Utah State states that “High fat content prevents adequate drying, increasing risk of rancidity” [1], and its food storage booklet names heat, light, oxygen and metal ions as accelerants of oxidative rancidity [17]. The peer-reviewed review is blunter: each added double bond in a polyunsaturated fatty acid at least doubles the oxidation rate, and lipid oxidation is “significantly faster in peanuts stored at water activities of 0.19 vs. 0.60” [67]. Freeze-dried food sits below that 0.19 figure by design. Drier is better against microbes and, for high-fat foods, not necessarily better against oxidation.

Moisture regain after a good cycle is a separate failure from a cycle that never finished. University of Minnesota Extension notes freeze-dried foods absorb moisture easily and must be packaged quickly [25]; Harvest Right states that food not placed in an airtight container “will begin to reabsorb moisture from the air and spoil” [18] and lists four causes of shortened shelf life: food not completely dry before packaging, delayed sealing after the cycle, incorrect oxygen absorber sizing, and inappropriate storage conditions [19]. Those four map onto the four sections that follow.

Check the container’s intended use

The largest single number in this whole diagnosis is the barrier gap between a vacuum-sealer bag and a foil laminate. IMPAK’s PAKVAC4.0 nylon/PE vacuum film publishes an oxygen transmission rate of 4.25 cc per 100 in² per 24 hours [28]; its PAKVF4 foil mylar publishes 0.001 cc per m² per 24 hours [27]. Those are different units — one square metre is roughly 1,550 square inches — and a reader who compares the two figures without converting understates the gap by about that factor. Convert before you draw a conclusion, and note that neither datasheet publishes the test temperature or relative humidity.

Utah State Extension states the general case without numbers: “Plastics are not that resistant to oxygen transfer and will allow significant oxygen levels into the container in 1 to 2 years”, and separately that “vacuum packaging is NOT a food preservation method by itself” [26]. Discount Mylar Bags scopes its own published barrier figures to the bare polyester layer and says the aluminum foil layer “provides the bulk of protection in a Mylar bag” [34]. PackFreshUSA puts it more sharply: “It is only the aluminum on the surface that keeps the oxygen out” [35].

That single sentence resolves most container failures. If the bag has a clear window, it has no foil across that window. IMPAK flags one of its own kraft window pouches with “This product does not have foil lining” [31], and its structure is published as front KPET/LLDPE, back Kraft/LLDPE [30]. ULINE’s kraft window pouch is sold as a barrier pouch with structure Paper/PET/NY/LLDPE — also no foil [32]. ULINE’s FoodSaver-compatible vacuum bags are 5-ply, 3 mil smooth and 8 mil embossed, and transparent throughout [33]. None of these publishes an oxygen transmission rate at all.

Container classPublished constructionPublished barrierWhat the source says it is forSource
Foil-laminate mylar, 4.3 mil48GaPET / PE / .00035 FOIL / LLDPEOTR 0.001 cc/m²/24 hrs; WVTR <0.0005 gr/100 in²/24 hrs; seal 400 °F / 40 PSI / 1 secLong-term barrier packaging[27]
Foil-laminate mylar, 7.5 mil48ga PET / .00035 Foil / 60ga BON / LLDPEOTR <0.0005 cc per 100 in²/24 hrs at 77 °F, 90% RH; seal 425 °FLong-term barrier packaging[29]
Kraft pouch with clear windowFront KPET/LLDPE, back Kraft/LLDPENot published; foil explicitly absentRetail presentation — the window is the point[30][31]
Kraft “barrier” pouch with windowPaper/PET/NY/LLDPENot published; no foil in the stackSold as a barrier pouch; barrier value unquantified[32]
Vacuum-sealer film (nylon/PE)60ga Nylon / adhesive / PEOTR 4.25 cc/100 in²/24 hrs; transparentVacuum packaging; no light barrier[28]
Embossed vacuum bag (FoodSaver-type)5-ply; polymer identities not publishedNot published; transparentFreezer, refrigerated, microwave, boil[33]

Penn State attaches storage life to the packaging class rather than the food: zip-top bags and plain containers give a few months; vacuum packaging in plastic gives 2 to 3 years because “plastic allows some permeability”; glass jars give many years, but only with an oxygen absorber or a vacuum seal; mylar requires both an absorber and a heat seal [24]. Utah State’s specification for freeze-dried storage is 5 to 7 mil mylar with no clear plastic window, plus an oxygen absorber [1].

Two container failures are commonly misread as barrier failures and are not. PackFreshUSA states that tiny breaks in the foil layer at creases “are not holes…their barrier properties are not significantly affected”, and that inside a metallized bag in a cool, dark place there is virtually no effect from light [35]. And a mylar bag is a liner, not a package: USA Emergency Supply states that “Mylar is not strongly resistant to insect penetration and not resistant at all to rodents” and must be used inside a more puncture-resistant container [36]. A chewed or punctured bag is a container-selection failure, not a seal failure.

Review absorber handling

Start with what an absorber does, because a false diagnosis below turns on it. PackFreshUSA states that “Oxygen absorbers do not absorb air; they absorb oxygen, which is 21% of air” [35], and puts the arithmetic plainly: “1/5 of the air volume will be gone but 4/5 of the air will always remain” [39].

Bag shrinkage is not proof that the absorber worked, and its absence is not proof that it failed. Wallaby Goods states that “It’s a misconception that a ‘vacuum-packed’ look confirms the oxygen has been removed” [48]. PackFreshUSA instructs readers not to expect all bags to have a vacuum-sealed look [56], and Discount Mylar Bags notes that powdery foods will not shrink and some freeze-dried items may not either, depending on air content [42]. Note that Wallaby contradicts itself across its own documents: a second Wallaby article says a properly sealed bag with enough absorbers will often feel slightly sucked in [49]. Recorded, not reconciled — but no source in this set offers suck-down as a verification method.

Sizing is by the residual air volume in the container, not by food weight. IMPAK states that “The size of oxygen absorber you need depends on the volume of the air in the package into which it is placed” [51], and its worked five-gallon calculation multiplies 3,066 cc of residual air by 0.21 to reach 628.53 cc of oxygen [45]. PackFreshUSA’s note on particle size is the one that changes behavior: “A pool filled with marbles will have the same interstitial air volume as one filled with basketballs” [37]. What matters is how much air the food class traps — PackFreshUSA publishes beans and rice at about 35 percent air, flour about 50 percent, and freeze-dried and pasta about 75 percent [38].

The published gallon recommendations span 8x, and freeze-dried is where the charts run out.

SourceOne-gallon recommendation as publishedCondition attachedSource
PackFreshUSA300 cc dense / 400 cc powder / 500 cc freeze-dried; 800 cc for an empty gallonAir-volume class; the 800 cc figure is for an empty container[37][38]
Discount Mylar Bags300 cc dense / 500 cc bulky or freeze-driedDry food below 10 percent moisture; round up, never down[42]
Harvest Right700 cc“For use in gallon-size Mylar bags” — no food class, no fill level[47]
Utah State Extension (2011)300 cc for a gallon or #10 can; 50 cc quart; 1,500 cc for five gallonsOctober 2011 fact sheet; the only university figures found[46]
Wallaby Goods400 cc; 400–500 cc for a gusset bagChart disclaimed as “only the average amount”[48]
IMPAK / Sorbent SystemsChart runs by bag dimension and stops at “Pasta and Thicker, less Dense Foods”No freeze-dried class published[45][51]

If the absorber is the suspect, these are the documented failure modes.

Failure modeWhat the source saysWhat you can check nowSource
Exposed too long before sealingPublished working windows run from 10 minutes to 90 minutes across suppliers; Utah State says use within 15 minutesNothing after the fact — this is a process record, not an inspection[40][46][43]
Spent on arrival or in the bag“A ‘spent’ (used) absorber will be brown and clumped together compared to a fresh pink or gray powder”Open one and feel it — soft and powdery, not hard and crunchy[46][41]
Undersized for the air volumeSizing is by residual air, and freeze-dried food is the highest-air class publishedRecompute from container volume, not food weight[45][51][38]
Rated capacity not deliveredIMPAK alleges some suppliers label by total air volume, so “what is a 500cc packet is actually a 100cc packet”Nothing without a test; IMPAK publishes a two-litre bottle protocol[44]
Stored open and reusedAbsorbers are single-use and cannot be reused once activated; store unused ones sealedCheck how the leftovers were kept — an airtight jar is the published method[50][43][40]
Indicator misreadPink or red means oxygen removed, blue means oxygen present — but purple is assigned opposite meanings by two suppliersTreat the indicator as weak evidence; the tactile check is the one PackFreshUSA prefers[41][44]
Aged in storagePackFreshUSA: “Oxygen absorbers dont get old, but if they become exposed to oxygen, they will fill up and wont work anymore”; Discount Mylar publishes 6 months to 2 years unopenedBoth positions are published; neither is reconciled[39][43]
Used with food above 10 percent moistureFoods above 10 percent moisture do not benefit, and reduced-oxygen packaging of moist food carries botulism riskA history question with a discard answer[46][42]

One mechanism worth knowing about, because it sits underneath the popular practice of adding a desiccant. IMPAK states that iron-based absorbers need “at least 65% relative humidity in the surrounding atmosphere before the rusting process can begin”, with a sodium activator enabling lower-humidity operation [51]. Freeze-dried food sits at a fraction of that humidity behind a vapor barrier. No manufacturer in this set publishes a low-humidity performance curve, so what that means for a real bag is unresolved.

Inspect the closure

The peer-reviewed review of heat-sealed flexible food packaging is the source with actual numbers here. It states that “Creases and wrinkles in the sealing surface…can act as capillary channels that may cause leaks”, and puts a figure on the pressure needed to close them: a minimum sealing pressure of 1.8 N/mm² was required for a leak-proof seal in the materials investigated [57]. The same review states that solid particle contamination “may cause microchannel formation and poor integrity throughout the sealing area”, that seal strength rises with dwell time and temperature, and — counterintuitively — that squeeze-out of molten sealant increases linearly with pressure [57].

For inspection, the FDA’s own container-integrity manual gives the method: “Use hand as well as eye…Rub thumb and forefinger around seal area, feeling for folds and ridges”, with a magnifying glass and proper illumination [59]. Its named defect classes for flexible pouches include channel leaks, nonbonding, wrinkles and seal creep [59]. Sanatron, an equipment manufacturer, states the limit of that method plainly: “Visual inspection is subjective, unreliable, operator dependent” [61].

Seal defect or causeWhat the source documentsHow to check itSource
Food dust or powder in the seal line“Even a light layer of dust, powder, oil, or moisture can interfere with proper bonding”; particle contamination forms microchannelsPre-seal checklist: no food particles trapped in the sealing area[58][57][55]
Wrinkles and creasesCapillary channels; 1.8 N/mm² minimum pressure to fill them; also caused by uneven jaw pressureLook for a seal line that is not continuous edge to edge[57][58][55]
Under-sealed — temperature or dwell too lowBelow the operating window the sealant does not melt enough for integrityPull the mouth of the bag open once cool; bend the top after cooling and watch for separation[57][36][54]
Burn-through — too hot“When the temperature is set too high for the bag material, it can easily cause deformation or create holes”; impulse sealers need experimentation to avoid burning throughLook for deformation, glossy or warped seal line[58][52][54]
Machine out of spec for the materialULINE rates its 12″ sealer to 8 mil for bags but caps metalized food bags at 2.5 mil, running at 446–464 °F; AIE reserves “plastic lined, foil and gusset bags” language for its 1,500 W double-impulse 20 mil unitCompare your bag’s rating against the machine’s, in the same units[60][62]
Total stack thickness misreadTop Mylar: “7-mil on each side = 14 mil total sealing thickness” — two walls, not one, meet the machine’s ratingDouble your per-side figure before comparing[52]
Worn consumables“A worn or damaged Teflon tape cover can allow direct heat contact with the bag”; failed heating element or wireInspect the PTFE cover and element[58]

On sealing temperature, the published guidance does not agree with itself, and the disagreement is worth seeing before you conclude your seal was fine. Top Mylar publishes 375–425 °F for 7-mil bags with a flat iron [52]. Wallaby publishes a wool setting in one article [53] and roughly 350 °F medium-high in another [54]. PackFreshUSA publishes a cotton setting with the steam function off, backed by a rigid surface [55]. USA Emergency Supply publishes a cotton, wool or high setting for about twenty seconds, and recommends experimenting on a leftover strip [36]. Discount Mylar Bags publishes 250–300 °F — but for the bare polyester layer, not the laminate [34], and IMPAK’s own laminate datasheets say 400 °F and 425 °F [27][29]. Following the 250–300 °F figure on a foil laminate under-seals it.

Whether a household vacuum sealer can close a mylar bag is disputed on mechanism, not on outcome. Wallaby says a FoodSaver “doesn’t get hot enough to work on Mylar material” [53]; Top Mylar attributes the same failure to the 14-mil stack [52]; PackFreshUSA, the largest bag seller in this set, explicitly endorses using a FoodSaver with the pump off to seal smaller bags [39]. Recorded, not reconciled. Wallaby also notes that hair straighteners work better with metal plates than ceramic ones [53].

One thing you cannot do at home: run a standard leak test. ASTM F1929 dye penetration is scoped to packages with edge seals formed between a transparent material and a porous sheet [63] — an opaque foil laminate is neither. The FDA’s pressurize-and-submerge method is destructive, requiring a needle puncture [59]. What remains are the mechanical checks: pull the cooled mouth open [36], bend the cooled top and watch for separation [54], run the visual continuity checklist [55], and — for a bag inside a bucket — fold it down until trapped air pillows up firmly and wait to see whether it deflates [36]. That last one has no published wait interval attached to it.

Storage conditions

Temperature has the one rate rule anyone publishes. Utah State Extension states: “For every 10.8 degrees in temperature rise you decrease the shelf life of stored food by half”, with a storage range of 40 to 60 °F and an instruction to avoid freezing temperatures [64]. The widely repeated 10-degree and 18-degree versions of that rule were not found in any extension or government source; only the 10.8 °F formulation is sourceable, and it is published as a bare assertion with no stated valid range or underlying data [64][65]. Clemson states separately that storage time “decreases significantly when temperatures are above 75 °F” [16], and the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints chart is conditioned on 75 °F or lower [68]. BYU notes attics and garages give a much shorter shelf life [69].

The one food where an extension service actually ran sensory panels shows what those figures mean in practice. For nonfat dry milk, Utah State reports off-flavors at 6 months and an unacceptable product at 24 months at 90 °F; unacceptable at 4 years at 70 °F; and minimal flavor change at 52 months at 50 °F [66]. Note that 70 °F sits inside the 75 °F ceiling under which the same product is charted at 15 to 20 years [68][69]. Taste failed long before the chart said it would.

Moisture ceiling for long-term storageAbout 10 percent or less moisture contentPackaging precondition; botulism risk above it under reduced oxygen[68][46][65]
Water activity for 12+ monthsBelow 0.6Regulatory reference values[70]
Insect controlFreeze at 0 °F for 3–4 daysInfested stored goods[64]

The duration claims themselves are contested, which matters when you are deciding whether a bag is old or merely stored badly. Utah State states that “no real data exists on the shelf-life of home freeze-dried products,” because the first home freeze dryer went on sale in 2013, and gives 8 to 10 years as a conservative estimate for commercially canned product in metal-mylar-type pouches [3]. Its January 2026 guide gives 10 to 15 years and sometimes up to 25 for commercial product, while recommending against home-preserved freeze-dried food beyond 5 to 10 years [1]. University of Minnesota gives up to 25 years for commercially prepared product and concedes limited information for home-prepared [25]. Harvest Right publishes up to 25 years, conditioned on airtight containers with oxygen absorbers away from moisture, heat and direct light, with no food-class breakdown and no temperature range [19]. In 2015, Oregon State’s answer of record was that no Extension or USDA information for home freeze-dried food existed at all [71].

Finally, the shelf-life figures in circulation are edibility figures, not taste figures. BYU says many dried foods “will have an acceptable taste for many years when stored at room temperature or below; however, some nutritional losses will occur”, and pairs its 30-plus year claims with a 7-year rotation recommendation [69]. If your stored food is edible and unpleasant, that is a documented outcome rather than a failure of your process.

What we could not source

  • No numeric light threshold, and no light-transmission figure for any finished bag. Extension sources say to store in the dark and stop there — no lux figures, no exposure durations, no vitamin-loss percentages [64][65]. On the packaging side, no manufacturer publishes a percent light-transmission figure for a finished food bag; the only optical number found anywhere is 3.0 percent haze for a bare polyester layer [34]. Light is the weakest-evidenced variable on this page.
  • “Residual oxygen below 2 percent” is not sourceable. The figures that are published are 0.01 percent with an absorber [46][47] and about 1 percent implied by nitrogen displacement [65]. The 2 percent figure appears to be vendor folklore and is not used here.
  • Package puffing is not a documented spoilage sign for dried or freeze-dried food. Bulging lids and gas bubbles are documented for canned goods [8][16]; no source in this set extends them to a mylar bag or dry pack.
  • There is no discard-on-history rule written for shelf-stable dry goods. Every history-based rule retrieved was written for refrigerated and frozen food during power outages [4][6][7]. For a bag of freeze-dried food with unknown storage history or a broken seal, the applicable guidance has to be borrowed from the general adage.
  • No recovery guidance exists for absorber failure or a lost seal. The six re-drying permissions [10][11][12][13][14][15] are written about condensation and moisture pickup. Harvest Right names incorrect absorber sizing as a cause of shortened shelf life but publishes no recovery procedure for it [19].
  • No manufacturer publishes an oxygen-absorber class for freeze-dried food. IMPAK’s and Wallaby’s charts stop at pasta and less-dense foods [45][48]; only PackFreshUSA’s 75-percent-air column [38] and Discount Mylar’s bulky/freeze-dried entry [42] cross the line. A per-food figure for freeze-dried fruit specifically does not exist in this set.
  • No mechanism is published for the one-absorber-per-bag rule. It appears as practice, never with a stated reason, and other suppliers recommend splitting across multiple packets [42][48].
  • No home-usable seal integrity standard was identified. ASTM F1929 excludes opaque foil laminates by its own scope [63], and the FDA’s submersion method is destructive [59]. The pillow-deflation check has no published wait interval [36].
  • No source ranks oxidation against microbial growth as the shelf-life limit for high-fat dried food. Utah State names rancidity as a risk [1][17]; Clemson and FSIS frame limits microbially [22][9]; nobody orders the two.
  • No peer-reviewed log-reduction data for home freeze-drying was retrieved. The statements that freeze-drying does not kill bacteria are extension and manufacturer assertions [1][2][3], not primary research findings; the candidate studies were paywalled or blocked.
  • Two on-topic extension documents could not be retrieved. An LSU AgCenter research-based FAQ on home freeze-drying and NCHFP’s own freeze-drying material were both located by title and URL, and neither could be fetched. Nothing on this page is attributed to either.
